title: Fly agaric
def: Fly agaric is a red or orange Amanita mushroom with white warts that is poisonous and related to the deadly Amanitas.
look: red or orange cap with white warts, white gills, a ring on the stem and a bulb at the base
warts are remnants of a veil and can wash off in rain
grows on the ground under birch and conifers
use: Learn it as a warning. Toxic. Related to the deadly Amanitas.
not: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo, an app, or this note. Spore prints, cutting it open, and an expert in person come first, and even then some look-alikes kill.
alike: Death cap: Olive-green to pale cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring and a cup (volva) at the base. One cap can kill. Symptoms start many hours later, after which it is already working on the liver
Destroying angel: Pure white cap, gills, ring and stem, with a cup at the base that may be buried. Deadly. Looks like button mushrooms and young puffballs
call: If someone may have eaten it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 for trouble breathing, seizures, or collapse.

title: Deadly galerina
def: Deadly galerina is a small brown mushroom on rotting wood that contains the same liver toxins as the death cap.
look: small brown mushroom on rotting wood with a thin ring and rusty brown spores
cap 1 to 4 cm, sticky when wet
rusty brown spore print
use: Learn it as a warning. Deadly. Grows on the same logs as honey mushrooms.
not: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo, an app, or this note. Spore prints, cutting it open, and an expert in person come first, and even then some look-alikes kill.
alike: Honey mushroom: Clusters of honey-coloured caps on wood with a ring; white spores. The deadly galerina looks like it
call: If someone may have eaten it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 for trouble breathing, seizures, or collapse.

title: Webcaps (Cortinarius)
def: Webcaps are brown Cortinarius mushrooms with a cobweb veil, and some damage the kidneys days after eating.
look: rusty-brown spores, a web-like veil on young caps, often on the ground in woods
rusty-brown spore print
cobweb-like veil between cap edge and stem on young caps
use: Learn it as a warning. Some are deadly to the kidneys. Never eat a brown mushroom you cannot identify.
not: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo, an app, or this note. Spore prints, cutting it open, and an expert in person come first, and even then some look-alikes kill.
alike: Chanterelle: Golden or orange funnel with blunt forked ridges that run down the stem, not true gills; fruity smell. Jack-o'-lantern has true gills, grows in clusters on wood and is toxic
call: If someone may have eaten it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 for trouble breathing, seizures, or collapse.

title: Chicken of the woods
def: Chicken of the woods is a bright orange and yellow shelf fungus on trees with pores, not gills.
look: bright orange and yellow shelves with no gills on trees, soft when young
no gills; tiny pores underneath
overlapping shelves on oak or other hardwood
use: Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. Some people react badly, and growths on conifers or eucalyptus can be harmful.
not: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo, an app, or this note. Spore prints, cutting it open, and an expert in person come first, and even then some look-alikes kill.
call: If someone may have eaten it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 for trouble breathing, seizures, or collapse.

title: Oyster mushroom
def: The oyster mushroom is a gray-tan shelf mushroom on wood with gills running down to a short side stem.

white to lilac spore print
grows in overlapping shelves on dead hardwood
use: Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. Do not confuse it with other shelf fungi that have gills.
not: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo, an app, or this note. Spore prints, cutting it open, and an expert in person come first, and even then some look-alikes kill.
